lesson.title: Throwing Good Money After Bad: Understanding the Sunk Cost Fallacy
lesson.summary: The sunk cost fallacy is the tendency to continue investing time, money, or effort into a decision because of resources already spent, even when those past costs cannot be recovered and should have no bearing on a rational choice about what to do next.
lesson.body:
A sunk cost is any resource, money, time, or effort, that has already been spent and cannot be recovered no matter what happens next. The sunk cost fallacy is the tendency to let the size of that unrecoverable investment influence a current decision, typically by continuing to invest further in a failing plan specifically because so much has already been put into it, rather than basing the decision purely on the expected costs and benefits that lie ahead. Sunk costs should logically be irrelevant to a rational decision about the future, since no choice made today can change what has already been spent, yet they exert a powerful and well documented psychological pull anyway.

A simple illustrative scenario captures the pattern clearly. Imagine buying a non-refundable movie ticket, then discovering thirty minutes in that the film is dull. The rational question going forward is simple: given the choice between spending the remaining ninety minutes watching a movie that is not enjoyable, or leaving to do anything else, which option leads to a better use of the time from this point on? The ticket price is gone either way, whether the movie is watched to the end or abandoned, so it has no bearing on that comparison. Yet many people stay anyway, reasoning that they already paid for it, treating the sunk cost of the ticket as though finishing the movie would somehow recover the spent money, when nothing about leaving early or staying changes how much was already spent.

The sunk cost fallacy persists partly because abandoning a failing course of action forces a person to consciously acknowledge that the earlier investment was, in some sense, wasted, and people are strongly motivated to avoid that admission. Continuing to invest, even in a losing effort, can feel like a way of postponing that admission, since walking away feels like converting a partial loss into a fully realized one, even though the size of the actual loss does not change either way. This connects to the broader theme running through cognitive biases generally: the error is not random or careless, it is a systematic, predictable pattern, which is exactly why the sunk cost fallacy shows up so reliably across very different contexts, from relationships to business decisions to personal hobbies.

The sunk cost fallacy has consequences well beyond a wasted movie ticket. Businesses sometimes keep funding a struggling project because of how much has already been invested in it, committing new resources to justify the old ones, even after new information makes clear the project is unlikely to succeed. Someone who has spent years training for a particular career path may stay in it well past the point where it is fulfilling, reasoning that leaving now would waste the years already spent, even though those years are gone regardless of what happens next, and the only real question is whether staying or switching offers a better path forward from today.

Together, the gambler's fallacy and the sunk cost fallacy show how the same broad category of cognitive bias can distort very different decisions, one skewing beliefs about random chance, the other skewing evaluations of an ongoing investment, while both trace back to the same story running through this set of concepts: the mind favors fast, intuitive shortcuts, whether perceiving an ambiguous image, attending to a crowded room, or judging a probability or a sunk investment, over slower, more accurate calculation, a trade-off that is usually efficient but is also, in predictable ways, sometimes wrong.
